books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note); Jefferson excerpt verified against Founders Online
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Missouri Compromise resolved sectional conflict over slavery, 1816-1836.

documents.title: The Tallmadge Amendment
documents.source: Debate on the Tallmadge Amendment, February 1819, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A New York congressman proposing terms for Missouri’s admission, in a House debate the Senate would reject.
documents.text: In February 1819, Representative James Tallmadge of New York proposed that Missouri enter the Union only if no more enslaved people were brought into the territory and the children of enslaved people were freed at age twenty-five. The House passed his amendment; the Senate rejected it, and the fight over Missouri began.

documents.title: Jefferson: a fire bell in the night
documents.source: Thomas Jefferson to John Holmes, April 22, 1820, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Jefferson writing privately from retirement at Monticello, a month after the Compromise passed.
documents.text: “but this momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror. I considered it at once as the knell of the Union. it is hushed indeed for the moment. but this is a reprieve only, not a final sentence. a geographical line, coinciding with a marked principle, moral and political, once conceived and held up to the angry passions of men, will never be obliterated; and every new irritation will mark it deeper and deeper.”

documents.title: The Missouri Compromise
documents.source: Missouri Compromise, March 1820, paraphrased from the statute. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The terms Congress agreed to after a year of debate over Missouri’s admission.
documents.text: The Compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine, carved from Massachusetts, as a free state, keeping the Senate balanced at twelve states each. It also barred slavery north of 36°30′ in the rest of the Louisiana territory, while allowing it south of that line.

documents.title: John Quincy Adams accepts the bargain
documents.source: John Quincy Adams, diary, March 1820, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Adams, then Secretary of State, writing privately about a compromise he accepted without liking.
documents.text: Adams wrote that he accepted the Missouri bargain because the Constitution gave Congress no power to end slavery inside a state, and the compromise was the most that could be had. He added that the slavery question would return, and that the line drawn over it would not hold the Union together by itself.

documents.title: The South Carolina Exposition and Protest
documents.source: South Carolina Exposition and Protest (John C. Calhoun, 1828), paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Calhoun, writing anonymously as Vice President, protesting the Tariff of 1828 and restating the states’-rights claim.
documents.text: The Exposition argued that the states had formed the Constitution as a compact, that each state kept the right to judge when the federal government overstepped it, and that a state could declare an unauthorized federal act void within its own borders. The claim was aimed at the tariff, not at slavery, but it showed sectional conflict finding a new issue eight years after Missouri.

documents.title: The Liberator demands immediate emancipation
documents.source: William Lloyd Garrison, The Liberator, first issue, January 1, 1831, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Garrison opening his abolitionist newspaper in Boston, rejecting gradual plans for ending slavery.
documents.text: Garrison announced that he would demand the immediate end of slavery, not a slow or gradual one, and that he would be heard on the question. His paper carried the slavery debate out of Congress and into the country at large, where it could not be settled by a bargain between states.

documents.title: The gag rule
documents.source: House of Representatives gag resolutions (Pinckney resolutions), December 1836, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The House majority voting to keep slavery petitions off its floor.
documents.text: The House resolved that every petition or resolution about slavery would be laid on the table without being read, printed, or debated. The rule stayed in force until 1844, and former president John Quincy Adams, then a member of the House, fought it in every session.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Missouri Compromise resolved sectional conflict over slavery, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of resolution does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Louisiana Purchase opening a vast territory, the balance of free and slave states, or the growth of cotton and Northern manufacturing.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument, such as the Tallmadge Amendment, the Compromise terms, or Jefferson’s letter.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents that show the conflict continuing after 1820.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Compromise Tariff of 1833 ending nullification, the Panic of 1819, or the American System’s tariff fights.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as Jefferson writing privately from retirement, or Calhoun writing anonymously as Vice President.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document’s author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where the Compromise worked and where it failed, or weighing its short peace against the conflicts that followed.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Missouri Compromise resolved the crisis of 1819-1820 but not the conflict behind it: it bought sixteen years of quiet by drawing a line over slavery, and the line itself kept the fight alive.
Context: The Louisiana Purchase had opened a vast territory, and Missouri’s application as a slave state threatened the eleven-to-eleven balance of free and slave states, while cotton in the South and manufacturing in the North pulled the sections apart.
Evidence it resolved: Document 3 gives the bargain, Missouri slave and Maine free with the 36°30′ line, and Document 4 shows Adams accepting it as the most the Constitution allowed; Document 1 shows how sharp the fight had been before the bargain.
Evidence it did not: Document 2 has Jefferson calling the quiet a reprieve, not a final sentence; Document 5 shows sectional conflict finding a new issue in the tariff by 1828; Document 6 carries the slavery debate out of Congress into the press; Document 7 shows the House banning the subject from its floor by 1836.
Beyond the documents: The Compromise Tariff of 1833 ended nullification the same way, by bargain rather than settlement, and the tariff fights of the 1820s show the same regional pattern.
Complexity: The Compromise worked as a truce and failed as a settlement: it kept the Union together in 1820 by freezing the question in geography, and the freeze is what made every later irritation mark the line deeper.
